statement: A [convex polyhedron](c:convex-polyhedron) in $\mathbb{R}^3$ whose faces are congruent [regular polygons](c:regular-polygon), with the same number of faces at every vertex (a [regular polyhedron](c:regular-polyhedron)), is similar to exactly one of five solids: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron or icosahedron. Each of the five exists.

hypotheses.text: The solid is a [convex polyhedron](c:convex-polyhedron) in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
All faces are congruent [regular polygons](c:regular-polygon), each with $p$ sides.
The same number $q$ of faces meets at every vertex.

conclusion: The pair $(p,q)$ is one of $(3,3)$, $(3,4)$, $(4,3)$, $(3,5)$, $(5,3)$, and the solid is similar to the tetrahedron, octahedron, cube, icosahedron or dodecahedron respectively; each of these five solids exists.

proofs.name: Euler count
proofs.slogan: Euler's formula turns the face and vertex counts into one relation between $p$ and $q$ that has five solutions, and each solution is realized once.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Uniqueness up to similarity rests on Cauchy's rigidity theorem; the other steps are proved in full.

roles.why: Convexity makes the surface a sphere, so Euler's formula holds, and every vertex has at least three faces.
The $p$-gon faces give $pF = 2E$, and their congruence fixes the shape of every face.
The count $q$ gives $qV = 2E$ and fixes the cyclic pattern of faces at every vertex.

steps.slogan: Count edges twice and combine the counts with Euler's formula.
steps.detail: Each edge borders two faces and has two ends, so $pF = 2E$ and $qV = 2E$. The [Euler characteristic](c:euler-characteristic) of a sphere is 2, so $V - E + F = 2$. Substituting gives $\frac1p + \frac1q = \frac12 + \frac1E$.

steps.slogan: List the integer pairs $(p,q)$ with $p,q \ge 3$ that satisfy the relation.
steps.detail: A face has at least 3 sides and a vertex of a convex polyhedron has at least 3 faces, so $p, q \ge 3$. Since $E > 0$, we get $\frac1p + \frac1q > \frac12$, that is $(p-2)(q-2) < 4$. This leaves $(3,3)$, $(3,4)$, $(4,3)$, $(3,5)$, $(5,3)$, with $E = 6, 12, 12, 30, 30$, $F = 2E/p$ and $V = 2E/q$.

steps.slogan: Show that each pair $(p,q)$ fixes the solid up to similarity.
steps.detail: Scale the edge length to 1. The counts $V$, $E$, $F$ and the cyclic pattern of $q$ faces at every vertex force the face-vertex structure of the tetrahedron, octahedron, cube, icosahedron or dodecahedron. A convex polyhedron is determined up to congruence by this structure and its face shapes (Cauchy's rigidity theorem).

steps.slogan: Construct each of the five solids by explicit vertex coordinates.
steps.detail: Take the cube $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$, the tetrahedron on four of its vertices (an even number of minus signs), the octahedron $(\pm1,0,0)$ with permutations, the icosahedron $(0,\pm1,\pm\varphi)$ with cyclic permutations, and the dodecahedron on the cube vertices together with $(0,\pm\varphi^{-1},\pm\varphi)$ and cyclic permutations. Here $\varphi$ is the golden ratio. A direct check gives congruent regular faces and $q$ faces at every vertex.

steps.slogan: Combine the steps into the list of five pairwise different solids.
steps.detail: By steps 2 and 3, every such solid is similar to one of five solids, one for each pair $(p,q)$. Step 4 shows that each of the five exists. The five pairs differ, so no two of the solids are similar.

concepts.c:convex-polyhedron: Convexity gives a spherical surface and at least three faces per vertex.
concepts.c:regular-polygon: Equal sides and angles of the faces fix the local geometry.
concepts.c:regular-polyhedron: The five solids are exactly the regular polyhedra.
concepts.c:euler-characteristic: The value 2 for the sphere gives the relation between $V$, $E$, $F$.

source.note: The classical angle-and-Euler count of the five regular solids (Euclid, Elements XIII, in modern form); uniqueness uses Cauchy's rigidity theorem.

statement: Let $(A_i)_{i \in I}$ be topological spaces and give $\prod_i A_i$ the [product topology](c:product-topology). Let $f_y \in \prod_i A_i$ for $y$ in a set $Y$ with a [filter](c:filter) $u$ (for example $\mathbb{N}$ with the cofinite filter), and let $g \in \prod_i A_i$. Then $f_y$ [converges](c:limit-of-a-sequence) to $g$ along $u$ if and only if $f_y(i)$ converges to $g(i)$ along $u$ for every $i \in I$.

hypotheses.text: The set $\prod_i A_i$ carries the [product topology](c:product-topology).
The points $f_y$ and $g$ lie in $\prod_i A_i$, and $u$ is a [filter](c:filter) on the index set $Y$.

conclusion: Convergence $f_y \to g$ along $u$ in the product holds if and only if $f_y(i) \to g(i)$ along $u$ in $A_i$ for every coordinate $i$.

proofs.name: Cylinder neighborhoods
proofs.slogan: The neighborhoods of $g$ in the product are generated by finite intersections of cylinders, so convergence in the product is convergence of each coordinate.
proofs.scope: Any index set $I$ and any filter $u$. For $I = \emptyset$ the product is one point and both sides hold.

roles.why: The [product topology](c:product-topology) makes the finite cylinders a neighborhood base and makes each projection continuous.
The filter $u$ is closed under finite intersections, which combines finitely many coordinate conditions.

steps.slogan: Describe the neighborhoods of $g$ by finite intersections of cylinders.
steps.detail: By definition of the product topology, the sets $\bigcap_{i \in J} \pi_i^{-1}(U_i)$, with $J \subseteq I$ finite and $U_i$ a neighborhood of $g(i)$, form a neighborhood base at $g$. In filter language, the neighborhood filter of $g$ is the infimum of the filters $\pi_i^{*}\,\mathcal{N}(g(i))$.

steps.slogan: Compose with each projection to get each coordinate limit.
steps.detail: Let $U$ be a neighborhood of $g(i)$. The projection $\pi_i$ is continuous, so $\pi_i^{-1}(U)$ is a neighborhood of $g$, and $f_y \in \pi_i^{-1}(U)$ for $u$-most $y$. That is, $f_y(i) \in U$ for $u$-most $y$.

steps.slogan: Combine finitely many coordinate conditions inside a basic neighborhood of $g$.
steps.detail: Assume every coordinate converges and take a basic neighborhood $\bigcap_{i \in J}\pi_i^{-1}(U_i)$. For each $i \in J$ we have $f_y(i) \in U_i$ for $u$-most $y$. A filter is closed under finite intersections, so $f_y$ lies in the basic set for $u$-most $y$.

steps.slogan: Join both directions into the equivalence for every index set.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives the implication from product convergence to coordinate convergence. Steps 1 and 3 give the converse, since every neighborhood of $g$ contains a basic one. Together they prove the equivalence.

concepts.c:product-topology: Its definition supplies the cylinder base and the continuous projections.
concepts.c:filter: Filters express the limit along $u$ and are closed under finite intersections.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-sequence: Convergence along $u$ is the notion compared in both directions.

source.note: mathlib rewrites with nhds_pi (the neighborhood filter of a product is the pi filter of the coordinate neighborhood filters) and Filter.tendsto_pi (a map into a pi filter converges iff each coordinate does).

statement: Let $X$ be a real [random variable](c:random-variable) on a probability space with $a \le X \le b$ almost surely. Then the [variance](c:variance) of $X$ is at most $\left(\frac{b-a}{2}\right)^2$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a real [random variable](c:random-variable) on a probability space.
The real numbers $a \le b$ satisfy $a \le X \le b$ almost surely.

proofs.name: Bhatia-Davis and completing the square
proofs.slogan: Bound the variance by $(b-\mu)(\mu-a)$ with the Bhatia-Davis argument, then complete the square in $\mu$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $a = b$, then $X$ is constant, the variance is 0, and the proof still applies.

roles.why: Boundedness and measurability make $X$ and $X^2$ integrable, so the [expectations](c:expectation-value) exist.
The two bounds make $(b-X)(X-a)$ nonnegative almost surely.

steps.slogan: Multiply the two bounds $b - X \ge 0$ and $X - a \ge 0$.
steps.detail: Almost surely $a \le X \le b$, so $(b-X)(X-a) \ge 0$. The variable $X$ is bounded, hence square integrable, so the [expectation](c:expectation-value) of this product exists and is nonnegative.

steps.slogan: Take expectations to bound the variance by $(b-\mu)(\mu-a)$.
steps.detail: With $\mu = \mathbb{E}[X]$, the inequality $0 \le \mathbb{E}[(b-X)(X-a)]$ reads $\mathbb{E}[X^2] \le (a+b)\mu - ab$. So $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu^2 \le (a+b)\mu - ab - \mu^2 = (b-\mu)(\mu-a)$, the Bhatia-Davis inequality.

steps.slogan: Complete the square to bound $(b-\mu)(\mu-a)$ by $((b-a)/2)^2$.
steps.detail: Put $m = (a+b)/2$ and $h = (b-a)/2$. Then $b - \mu = h - (\mu - m)$ and $\mu - a = h + (\mu - m)$, so the product equals $h^2 - (\mu-m)^2 \le h^2$.

concepts.c:random-variable: $X$ is the bounded variable whose spread is bounded.
concepts.c:variance: The variance is the quantity that the proof bounds.
concepts.c:expectation-value: Taking expectations of the pointwise inequality gives the bound.

source.note: mathlib uses variance_le_sub_mul_sub (Bhatia-Davis), rewrites the bound by ring as $h^2 - (\mu - m)^2$, and drops the square with sub_le_self.

statement: Let $n \ge 1$. A complex number $\zeta$ is a [primitive](c:is-primitive-root) $n$-th [root of unity](c:root-of-unity) (that is, $\zeta^n = 1$ and $\zeta^m \ne 1$ for $0 < m < n$) if and only if $\zeta = e^{2\pi i k/n}$ for some integer $k$ with $0 \le k < n$ whose [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor) with $n$ is 1.

hypotheses.text: The integer $n$ is at least 1.

conclusion: The primitive $n$-th roots of unity are exactly the numbers $e^{2\pi i k/n}$ with $0 \le k < n$ and $\gcd(k,n) = 1$.

proofs.name: Powers of a generator
proofs.slogan: Every $n$-th root of unity is a power of $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$, and $\omega^k$ has order $n/\gcd(k,n)$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for every $n \ge 1$. For $n = 1$ the only value is $k = 0$ and $\zeta = 1$.

roles.why: A positive $n$ makes $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$ defined and the polynomial $z^n - 1$ of degree $n$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$ is a [primitive](c:is-primitive-root) $n$-th root of unity.
steps.detail: We have $\omega^m = e^{2\pi i m/n}$, and this equals 1 exactly when $m/n$ is an integer, that is when $n \mid m$. So $\omega^n = 1$ and no smaller positive power of $\omega$ equals 1.

steps.slogan: Show that every $n$-th root of unity is $\omega^k$ with $0 \le k < n$.
steps.detail: By step 1 the numbers $\omega^0, \dots, \omega^{n-1}$ are distinct, and each is a root of $z^n - 1$. This polynomial has degree $n$ and so at most $n$ roots, which are therefore exactly these numbers.

steps.slogan: Compute the order of $\omega^k$ as $n/\gcd(k,n)$.
steps.detail: Let $d = \gcd(k,n)$. Then $(\omega^k)^m = 1$ iff $n \mid km$ iff $(n/d) \mid (k/d)\,m$ iff $(n/d) \mid m$, since $k/d$ and $n/d$ are coprime. So the order of $\omega^k$ is $n/d$.

steps.slogan: Select the powers of order $n$ to finish the proof.
steps.detail: The root $\omega^k$ is primitive iff $n/d = n$ iff $\gcd(k,n) = 1$. With step 2, every primitive $n$-th root has the form $\omega^k$ with $0 \le k < n$ and $\gcd(k,n)=1$, and each such $\omega^k$ is primitive.

concepts.c:is-primitive-root: A primitive root has order exactly $n$, which the proof characterizes.
concepts.c:root-of-unity: The proof lists all $n$-th roots of unity as powers of $\omega$.
concepts.c:greatest-common-divisor: The gcd of $k$ and $n$ gives the order $n/\gcd(k,n)$.

source.note: mathlib shows that exp(2 pi i / n) is primitive (isPrimitiveRoot_exp), writes zeta as a power of it (IsPrimitiveRoot.eq_pow_of_pow_eq_one), and reads coprimality from IsPrimitiveRoot.pow_iff_coprime.

statement: For any four points $A, B, C, D$ of a real [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) (for example the Euclidean plane or space), $|AC|\cdot|BD| \le |AB|\cdot|CD| + |BC|\cdot|AD|$.

hypotheses.text: The points lie in a real [inner product space](c:inner-product-space), with distance $|XY| = \|X - Y\|$.

proofs.name: Inversion
proofs.slogan: Invert $B$, $C$, $D$ in the unit sphere around $A$ and apply the triangle inequality to the three images.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $A$ equals $B$, $C$ or $D$ the inequality is direct; otherwise the proof inverts about $A$.

roles.why: The inner product gives the norm identity for inverted points, and the norm satisfies the triangle inequality.

steps.slogan: Settle the cases where $A$ coincides with $B$, $C$ or $D$ directly.
steps.detail: If $B = A$, both sides equal $|AC||AD|$. If $C = A$, the left side is 0. If $D = A$, both sides equal $|AB||AC|$.

steps.slogan: Map $B$, $C$, $D$ to $B'$, $C'$, $D'$ by inversion in the unit sphere around $A$.
steps.detail: Assume $B, C, D \ne A$. For $X \in \{B, C, D\}$ put $X' = A + (X - A)/|X - A|^2$.

steps.slogan: Compute $|X'Y'| = |XY|/(|AX||AY|)$ for two inverted points.
steps.detail: Let $u = X - A$ and $v = Y - A$. Expanding with the [inner product](c:inner-product-space) gives $\left|\frac{u}{|u|^2} - \frac{v}{|v|^2}\right|^2 = \frac{1}{|u|^2} - \frac{2\langle u,v\rangle}{|u|^2|v|^2} + \frac{1}{|v|^2} = \frac{|u-v|^2}{|u|^2|v|^2}$.

steps.slogan: Apply the triangle inequality $|B'D'| \le |B'C'| + |C'D'|$ to the inverted points.
steps.detail: The triangle inequality holds for the norm of the inner product space. By step 3, it says that $\frac{|BD|}{|AB||AD|} \le \frac{|BC|}{|AB||AC|} + \frac{|CD|}{|AC||AD|}$.

steps.slogan: Multiply by $|AB||AC||AD|$ to clear the denominators and finish.
steps.detail: Multiplying by the positive number $|AB||AC||AD|$ gives $|AC||BD| \le |AD||BC| + |AB||CD|$. With the degenerate cases of step 1, this is the claim for all four points.

concepts.c:inner-product-space: The inner product gives the distance formula for inverted points.

source.note: mathlib treats the cases b, c or d equal to a, then applies dist_triangle to the inversions of b, c, d about a (dist_inversion_inversion) and clears denominators.

statement: Let $\gamma,\tilde\gamma$ be unit-speed [geodesics](c:geodesic) in [Riemannian manifolds](c:riemannian-manifold) $M,\tilde M$ of equal dimension, with normal [Jacobi fields](c:jacobi-field) $J,\tilde J$ such that $J(0)=\tilde J(0)=0$ and $|J'(0)|=|\tilde J'(0)|$. If $\tilde\gamma$ has no conjugate point in $(0,T]$ and the [sectional curvatures](c:sectional-curvature) of $\tilde M$ along $\tilde\gamma$ are at least those of $M$ along $\gamma$, then $|\tilde J|\le|J|$.

hypotheses.text: The curves $\gamma$ and $\tilde\gamma$ are unit-speed [geodesics](c:geodesic) of [Riemannian manifolds](c:riemannian-manifold) $M$ and $\tilde M$ of equal dimension.
$J$ and $\tilde J$ are normal [Jacobi fields](c:jacobi-field) with $J(0)=\tilde J(0)=0$ and $|J'(0)|=|\tilde J'(0)|$.
For every $t$, each [sectional curvature](c:sectional-curvature) of $\tilde M$ at $\tilde\gamma(t)$ of a plane containing $\tilde\gamma'(t)$ is at least each such curvature of $M$ at $\gamma(t)$.
The geodesic $\tilde\gamma$ has no point conjugate to $\tilde\gamma(0)$ in $(0,T]$.

proofs.name: Index lemma
proofs.slogan: Transplant $J$ into $\tilde M$ by parallel frames, compare index forms by curvature, and use the index lemma to show that $|J|/|\tilde J|$ increases.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $\dim M=\dim\tilde M$; the proof also works for $\dim M\le\dim\tilde M$. The index lemma is quoted, not reproved.

roles.why: The two geodesics carry parallel orthonormal frames of the same size, which transplant fields from $M$ to $\tilde M$.
Equal initial speeds start the ratio $|J|/|\tilde J|$ at 1, and normality makes the curvature terms sectional curvatures.
The curvature inequality turns the index form of the transplanted field into a lower bound by the index form of $J$.
Without conjugate points on $\tilde\gamma$ the index lemma applies, and $\tilde J$ has no zero in $(0,T]$.

steps.slogan: Reduce to $J'(0) \ne 0$ and study the ratio $|J|/|\tilde J|$ on $(0,T]$.
steps.detail: If $J'(0)=0$, then $J=\tilde J=0$ and nothing is to prove. Otherwise $\tilde J\ne0$ on $(0,T]$, because a zero would be a conjugate point, and $|J(t)|/|\tilde J(t)|\to|J'(0)|/|\tilde J'(0)|=1$ as $t\to0^+$.

steps.slogan: Transplant $J$ to a field $V$ along $\tilde\gamma$ using parallel orthonormal frames.
steps.detail: Fix $t_0$ with $J(t_0)\ne0$ and choose [parallel](c:parallel-transport) orthonormal frames $E_i$ along $\gamma$ and $\tilde E_i$ along $\tilde\gamma$ with $E_n=\gamma'$, $\tilde E_n=\tilde\gamma'$, $E_1(t_0)\parallel J(t_0)$ and $\tilde E_1(t_0)\parallel\tilde J(t_0)$. Write $J=\sum a_iE_i$ and set $V=c\sum a_i\tilde E_i$ with $c=|\tilde J(t_0)|/|J(t_0)|$. Then $V(0)=0$, $V(t_0)=\tilde J(t_0)$, $|V'|=c|J'|$ and $|V|=c|J|$.

steps.slogan: Compare the index forms by the curvature inequality to get $\tilde I(V,V)\le c^2I(J,J)$.
steps.detail: Both fields are normal, so $\langle\tilde R(\tilde\gamma',V)\tilde\gamma',V\rangle=\tilde K|V|^2\ge Kc^2|J|^2=c^2\langle R(\gamma',J)\gamma',J\rangle$ by the hypothesis on [sectional curvature](c:sectional-curvature). With $|V'|=c|J'|$ this gives $\tilde I(V,V)\le c^2I(J,J)=c^2\langle J',J\rangle(t_0)$.

steps.slogan: Apply the index lemma on $\tilde\gamma$ to bound $\tilde I(\tilde J,\tilde J)$ by $\tilde I(V,V)$.
steps.detail: The geodesic $\tilde\gamma$ has no conjugate point in $(0,t_0]$, and $V$ and $\tilde J$ are normal with equal ends, so the index lemma gives $\langle\tilde J',\tilde J\rangle(t_0)=\tilde I(\tilde J,\tilde J)\le\tilde I(V,V)$. The first equality is integration by parts for a [Jacobi field](c:jacobi-field).

steps.slogan: Combine the last two steps into $\langle J',J\rangle/|J|^2\ge\langle\tilde J',\tilde J\rangle/|\tilde J|^2$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $\langle\tilde J',\tilde J\rangle(t_0)\le c^2\langle J',J\rangle(t_0)$ with $c^2=|\tilde J(t_0)|^2/|J(t_0)|^2$. Dividing by $|\tilde J(t_0)|^2$ shows $\frac{d}{dt}\log\frac{|J|}{|\tilde J|}\ge0$ at every $t_0$ with $J(t_0)\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Integrate from $0$ and exclude zeros of $J$ to conclude $|J|\ge|\tilde J|$.
steps.detail: On $(0,t^*)$, where $t^*$ is the first zero of $J$ (if any), the ratio is nondecreasing with limit 1 at 0, so $|J|\ge|\tilde J|$. A zero at $t^*$ would give $0=|J(t^*)|\ge|\tilde J(t^*)|>0$, which is false, so $J$ has no zero and the inequality holds on $[0,T]$.

concepts.c:geodesic: The Jacobi fields live along the two geodesics being compared.
concepts.c:riemannian-manifold: The comparison is between two Riemannian manifolds of equal dimension.
concepts.c:jacobi-field: The fields $J$ and $\tilde J$ measure how nearby geodesics spread.
concepts.c:sectional-curvature: The curvature inequality is what drives the comparison of index forms.
concepts.c:parallel-transport: Parallel frames identify the two tangent spaces along the curves.

source.note: The textbook proof by the index lemma: M. P. do Carmo, Riemannian Geometry (Birkhauser, 1992), Chapter 10; J. Cheeger and D. G. Ebin, Comparison Theorems in Riemannian Geometry (North-Holland, 1975), Chapter 1.

statement: Let $F$ be a field that is not [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field) and whose [algebraic closure](c:algebraic-closure) $\bar F$ is a finite extension of $F$. Then $\operatorname{char}F=0$, $\bar F=F(\sqrt{-1})$ and $[\bar F:F]=2$, and $F$ is real closed: $F$ is [formally real](c:formally-real-field) and has no proper formally real algebraic extension.

hypotheses.text: The [algebraic closure](c:algebraic-closure) $\bar F$ has finite degree over $F$.
The field $F$ is not [algebraically closed](c:algebraically-closed-field), that is $\bar F\ne F$.

conclusion: The field $F$ has characteristic 0 and is real closed, with $\bar F=F(\sqrt{-1})$ of degree 2 over $F$.

proofs.name: Artin-Schreier outline
proofs.slogan: Galois theory with Sylow subgroups, Artin-Schreier extensions and Kummer theory forces $[\bar F:F]=2$, and then the squares give the ordering.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Artin-Schreier proof: steps 2 to 4 rest on the cited paper, and steps 1, 5 and 6 are proved here. The theorem is one member of the real closed field family, whose equivalent definitions use orderings and odd-degree roots.

roles.why: Finiteness of $\bar F/F$ makes the Galois group finite, so Sylow subgroups exist.
The assumption $\bar F\ne F$ makes the Galois group nontrivial and excludes degree 1.

steps.slogan: Show that $F$ is perfect, so that $\bar F/F$ is a finite [Galois](c:galois-extension) extension.
steps.detail: In characteristic $p$, if $a\in F$ is not a $p$-th power, then $x^{p^k}-a$ is irreducible for all $k$, which contradicts finiteness of $[\bar F:F]$. So $F$ is perfect, $\bar F/F$ is separable and hence Galois, with a finite group $G\ne1$.

steps.slogan: Rule out positive characteristic with Artin-Schreier extensions.
steps.detail: The cited proof uses the description of cyclic extensions of degree $p$ in characteristic $p$ by equations $x^p-x=a$ to show that $\bar F/F$ cannot have a finite nontrivial Galois group there. So $\operatorname{char}F=0$.

steps.slogan: Use Sylow subgroups and Kummer theory to show that $|G|$ has no odd prime factor.
steps.detail: For an odd prime $p$ dividing $|G|$, the fixed field $E$ of a [Sylow subgroup](c:sylow-subgroup) contains a primitive $p$-th root of unity, since $[E(\zeta_p):E]$ is a power of $p$ and divides $p-1$. Kummer theory then describes the cyclic degree-$p$ layers by radicals and gives a contradiction. So $G$ is a 2-group.

steps.slogan: Show that $\bar F=F(\sqrt{-1})$ by the same argument for $p=2$.
steps.detail: Let $E=F(\sqrt{-1})$, which contains a primitive 4th root of unity. The Sylow-Kummer argument with $p=2$ over $E$ shows that $\bar F/E$ has trivial group, so $\bar F=E$. Since $\bar F\ne F$, we get $\sqrt{-1}\notin F$ and $[\bar F:F]=2$.

steps.slogan: Show that sums of squares are squares and that the squares order $F$.
steps.detail: Given $a,b\in F$, pick $c,d\in F$ with $(c+d\sqrt{-1})^2=a+b\sqrt{-1}$; taking norms gives $a^2+b^2=(c^2+d^2)^2$. So sums of squares are squares, and $-1$ is not a square, so $F$ is [formally real](c:formally-real-field). The same square-root computation gives $a=c^2-d^2$ with $cd=0$ for each $a\in F$, so every element is $\pm$ a square and the squares are the positive cone of an [ordered field](c:ordered-field) structure.

steps.slogan: Show that $F$ has no proper formally real algebraic extension.
steps.detail: An algebraic extension of $F$ embeds in $\bar F=F(\sqrt{-1})$, so it equals $F$ or $F(\sqrt{-1})$. The field $F(\sqrt{-1})$ is not formally real, since $-1$ is a square there. With step 5, the field $F$ is real closed.

concepts.c:algebraic-closure: Its finite degree over $F$ is the hypothesis of the theorem.
concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: The field $F$ is assumed not to be algebraically closed.
concepts.c:galois-extension: Perfectness makes the finite extension Galois, so group theory applies.
concepts.c:sylow-subgroup: Sylow subgroups reduce the argument to prime-power layers.
concepts.c:formally-real-field: The proof shows that $-1$ is not a sum of squares in $F$.
concepts.c:ordered-field: The squares define the ordering that makes $F$ real closed.

source.ref: E. Artin and O. Schreier, Eine Kennzeichnung der reell abgeschlossenen Koerper, Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universitaet Hamburg 5 (1927), 225-231
source.note: Steps 1 to 4 follow the structure of the published proof as presented in textbooks such as S. Lang, Algebra, Chapter XI; step 5 is the elementary conclusion.

statement: Let $J\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a [Jordan curve](c:jordan-curve). Then there is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) of $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto itself that maps $J$ onto the unit circle.

hypotheses.text: The set $J$ is a [Jordan curve](c:jordan-curve): a homeomorphic image of the circle in the plane.

conclusion: Some [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) of the plane takes $J$ onto the unit circle; hence the closure of the bounded component of $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus J$ is a closed disk.

proofs.name: Conformal maps and gluing
proofs.slogan: Map both complementary domains conformally onto the two sides of the unit circle, extend the maps to the boundary, and match them by a circle homeomorphism.
proofs.scope: The planar case (Jordan-Schoenflies). In dimension 3 the statement fails for wild spheres such as the Alexander horned sphere.

roles.why: The Jordan curve is the common boundary of two Jordan domains, and Carathéodory's theorem needs exactly this.

steps.slogan: Split the Riemann sphere along $J$ into two simply connected domains.
steps.detail: The Jordan curve theorem gives two components $U$ (bounded) and $V$ of $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus J$, each with boundary $J$. In the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere), $U$ and $V\cup\{\infty\}$ are [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space), because the complement of each is the connected closure of the other.

steps.slogan: Map $U$ and $V\cup\{\infty\}$ conformally onto the two sides of the unit circle.
steps.detail: The Riemann mapping theorem gives conformal maps $f\colon\mathbb{D}\to U$ and $g\colon\hat{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\overline{\mathbb{D}}\to V\cup\{\infty\}$ with $g(\infty)=\infty$.

steps.slogan: Extend $f$ and $g$ to homeomorphisms of the closed domains by Carathéodory's theorem.
steps.detail: The common boundary $J$ is a Jordan curve, so Carathéodory's theorem extends $f$ to a homeomorphism $\bar f\colon\overline{\mathbb{D}}\to\bar U$. For $g$, a Möbius map first moves $V\cup\{\infty\}$ to a bounded domain, and the same argument gives $\bar g\colon\hat{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\mathbb{D}\to\bar V\cup\{\infty\}$.

steps.slogan: Extend the circle homeomorphism $h=\bar g^{-1}\circ\bar f|_{S^1}$ radially to the outside.
steps.detail: Both maps restrict to homeomorphisms of the circle onto $J$, so $h=\bar g^{-1}\circ\bar f|_{S^1}$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) of $S^1$. Define $H(rz)=r\,h(z)$ for $r\ge1$ and $|z|=1$, and $H(\infty)=\infty$; this is a homeomorphism of $\hat{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\mathbb{D}$ that equals $h$ on $S^1$.

steps.slogan: Glue $\bar f$ and $\bar g\circ H$ into one homeomorphism $\Phi$ that fixes $\infty$.
steps.detail: On $S^1$ we have $\bar g\circ H=\bar g\circ h=\bar f$, so $\Phi=\bar f$ on $\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ and $\Phi=\bar g\circ H$ outside $\mathbb{D}$ is a continuous bijection of the sphere, hence a homeomorphism by compactness. It fixes $\infty$ and maps $S^1$ onto $J$, so $\Phi^{-1}$ restricted to $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a homeomorphism of the plane taking $J$ onto the unit circle.

concepts.c:jordan-curve: The curve $J$ is the common boundary of the two domains.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The proof builds a homeomorphism of the plane from boundary extensions.
concepts.c:riemann-sphere: The sphere makes the exterior domain simply connected with $\infty$ inside.
concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Simple connectivity of both domains allows the Riemann mapping theorem.

source.note: The classical proof by the Riemann mapping theorem and Caratheodory's boundary theorem (Ch. Pommerenke, Boundary Behaviour of Conformal Maps, Springer 1992, Chapter 2); C. Thomassen, Amer. Math. Monthly 99 (1992), 116-130, gives an elementary proof.

statement: Let $f\colon\alpha\to\beta\to\beta$ be left commutative: $f\,x\,(f\,y\,z)=f\,y\,(f\,x\,z)$ for all $x,y,z$. Then for every finite [list](c:list) $l$ and every $b\in\beta$, the left [fold](c:fold) of $l$ with $\operatorname{flip}f$ and start $b$ equals the right fold of $l$ with $f$ and start $b$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is left commutative: $f\,x\,(f\,y\,z)=f\,y\,(f\,x\,z)$ for all $x,y,z$.
The [list](c:list) $l$ is finite, built from the empty list by adding elements.

proofs.name: Induction on the list
proofs.slogan: Induct on the list with the start value generalized, and move $f\,a$ out of the right fold by left commutativity.
proofs.scope: All lists and all start values. Without left commutativity the left side equals the right fold of the [reversed list](c:list-reversal); the two-operation form of the second duality theorem has the same proof.

roles.why: Left commutativity lets the first application of $f$ move to the outside of the right fold.
The finite list is built by nil and cons, which supports induction on $l$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\operatorname{foldr}(f,f\,a\,b,l)=f\,a\,(\operatorname{foldr}(f,b,l))$ for every $l$.
steps.detail: Induct on $l$. For $l=[\,]$ both sides equal $f\,a\,b$. For $l=x::l'$, the induction hypothesis rewrites the left side to $f\,x\,(f\,a\,(\operatorname{foldr}(f,b,l')))$, and left commutativity swaps $x$ and $a$.

steps.slogan: Check that both folds return $b$ on the empty list.
steps.detail: By the definition of the two [folds](c:fold), both sides equal $b$ when the list is empty. This is the base case of the induction on $l$.

steps.slogan: Peel off the first element $a$ and apply the hypothesis with start value $f\,a\,b$.
steps.detail: By definition, $\operatorname{foldl}(\operatorname{flip}f,b,a::l)=\operatorname{foldl}(\operatorname{flip}f,f\,a\,b,l)$. The induction hypothesis holds for every start value, so this equals $\operatorname{foldr}(f,f\,a\,b,l)$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite with the lemma to reach $\operatorname{foldr}(f,b,a::l)$.
steps.detail: By step 1, $\operatorname{foldr}(f,f\,a\,b,l)=f\,a\,(\operatorname{foldr}(f,b,l))$, which is $\operatorname{foldr}(f,b,a::l)$ by definition. With step 2 this completes the induction.

concepts.c:list: The induction runs over the structure of the list.
concepts.c:fold: Both sides of the identity are folds of the same list.
concepts.c:list-reversal: Reversal is what left commutativity makes invisible.

source.note: mathlib inducts on the list generalizing the start value, and simp uses foldr_cons_eq_foldr_apply, the lemma of step 1, which needs LeftCommutative.

statement: Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional [central simple algebra](c:central-simple-algebra) over a field $k$, let $B$ be a finite-dimensional [simple algebra](c:simple-algebra) over $k$, and let $f,g\colon B\to A$ be unital $k$-algebra homomorphisms. Then there is a unit $u\in A$ with $g(b)=u\,f(b)\,u^{-1}$ for all $b\in B$. In particular every $k$-automorphism of $A$ is an [inner automorphism](c:inner-automorphism).

hypotheses.text: The algebra $A$ is a finite-dimensional [central simple algebra](c:central-simple-algebra) over $k$.
The algebra $B$ is a finite-dimensional [simple algebra](c:simple-algebra) over $k$.
The maps $f,g\colon B\to A$ are unital $k$-algebra homomorphisms.

conclusion: A unit $u\in A$ exists with $g(b)=u\,f(b)\,u^{-1}$ for all $b$; taking $B=A$ and $f=\mathrm{id}$ shows that every $k$-automorphism of $A$ is inner.

proofs.name: Two module structures
proofs.slogan: Make $A$ a module over $A\otimes B^{\mathrm{op}}$ in two ways, via $f$ and via $g$; the modules are isomorphic and the isomorphism is multiplication by $u$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for finite-dimensional $A$ and $B$ and unital $f,g$. The case $B=A$, $f=\mathrm{id}$ gives that automorphisms are inner.

roles.why: The center of $A$ is $k$, which makes $A\otimes B^{\mathrm{op}}$ simple.
A simple $B^{\mathrm{op}}$ makes the tensor algebra simple, so it has one simple module.
The homomorphisms $f$ and $g$ define the two module actions and give the final conjugation.

steps.slogan: Show that $S=A\otimes_kB^{\mathrm{op}}$ is a simple finite-dimensional algebra.
steps.detail: A tensor product of a [central simple algebra](c:central-simple-algebra) with a simple algebra is simple, and $B^{\mathrm{op}}$ is simple. Also $\dim_kS=\dim A\cdot\dim B$ is finite.

steps.slogan: Let $a\otimes b$ act on $A$ by $x\mapsto a\,x\,f(b)$, and by $x\mapsto a\,x\,g(b)$.
steps.detail: Both rules are $k$-bilinear and compatible with products in $S$, because $f(b')f(b)=f(b'b)$ gives the order reversal that $B^{\mathrm{op}}$ needs. Write $A_f$ and $A_g$ for the two $S$-modules; both have $k$-dimension $\dim A$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $A_f\cong A_g$ because a simple algebra has one simple module.
steps.detail: By the Artin-Wedderburn theorem, $S\cong M_m(D)$ has a unique simple module up to isomorphism, and every finite-dimensional module is a direct sum of copies of it. So $S$-modules of equal dimension are isomorphic, and we get a bijective $k$-linear $\varphi\colon A\to A$ with $\varphi(a\,x\,f(b))=a\,\varphi(x)\,g(b)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi(x)=x\,w$ for $w=\varphi(1)$ and that $w$ is a unit.
steps.detail: Taking $b=1$ gives $\varphi(ax)=a\varphi(x)$, so $\varphi(x)=x\,w$ with $w=\varphi(1)$. Since $\varphi$ is onto, $xw=1$ for some $x$, and in a finite-dimensional algebra a right inverse is a two-sided inverse.

steps.slogan: Evaluate $\varphi(f(b))$ in two ways to get conjugation by $u=w^{-1}$.
steps.detail: Taking $a=1$ and $x=1$ gives $\varphi(f(b))=w\,g(b)$, and step 4 gives $\varphi(f(b))=f(b)\,w$. So $f(b)\,w=w\,g(b)$, that is $g(b)=u\,f(b)\,u^{-1}$ with $u=w^{-1}$.

concepts.c:central-simple-algebra: Centrality and simplicity of $A$ make the tensor algebra simple.
concepts.c:simple-algebra: Simplicity of $B$ makes $B^{\mathrm{op}}$ and the tensor algebra simple.
concepts.c:inner-automorphism: The conclusion says that every automorphism is conjugation by a unit.

source.note: The standard module-theoretic proof of the Skolem-Noether theorem for central simple algebras, using that $A\otimes B^{op}$ is simple.

statement: Let $\varphi$ be a [Schwartz function](c:schwartz-function) on $\mathbb{R}$. Then $\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x\pm i\varepsilon}\,dx=\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x}\,dx\mp i\pi\varphi(0)$, where $\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int\frac{\varphi(x)}{x}dx=\lim_{\delta\to0^+}\int_{|x|>\delta}\frac{\varphi(x)}{x}dx$ is the [Cauchy principal value](c:cauchy-principal-value). As [distributions](c:distribution), $\frac1{x\pm i0}=\mathrm{p.v.}\frac1x\mp i\pi\delta$.

hypotheses.text: The function $\varphi$ is a [Schwartz function](c:schwartz-function): smooth and rapidly decreasing with all derivatives.

conclusion: $\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\int\frac{\varphi(x)}{x\pm i\varepsilon}dx=\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int\frac{\varphi(x)}{x}dx\mp i\pi\varphi(0)$, with the same sign choice on both sides.

proofs.name: Real and imaginary parts
proofs.slogan: Split $1/(x\pm i\varepsilon)$ into real and imaginary parts and send each to its limit by dominated convergence.
proofs.scope: The real-line version for Schwartz test functions. The Plemelj formulas for Cauchy integrals along a contour are the other member of the family.

roles.why: Boundedness of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$ and fast decay give the dominating functions in both limits.

steps.slogan: Split the kernel as $\frac{x}{x^2+\varepsilon^2}\mp\frac{i\varepsilon}{x^2+\varepsilon^2}$.
steps.detail: Multiplying numerator and denominator by $x\mp i\varepsilon$ gives $\frac1{x\pm i\varepsilon}=\frac{x}{x^2+\varepsilon^2}\mp\frac{i\varepsilon}{x^2+\varepsilon^2}$. We integrate $\varphi$ against each part.

steps.slogan: Rescale $x=\varepsilon t$ and apply dominated convergence to the imaginary part.
steps.detail: We have $\int\frac{\varepsilon\,\varphi(x)}{x^2+\varepsilon^2}dx=\int\frac{\varphi(\varepsilon t)}{1+t^2}dt$. The integrand is bounded by $\sup|\varphi|/(1+t^2)$, which is integrable, and tends to $\varphi(0)/(1+t^2)$, so the limit is $\pi\varphi(0)$.

steps.slogan: Subtract $\varphi(0)$ near $0$ using the oddness of $x/(x^2+\varepsilon^2)$.
steps.detail: The function $x/(x^2+\varepsilon^2)$ is odd, so $\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{x\,\varphi(0)}{x^2+\varepsilon^2}dx=0$. We may therefore subtract this term and split the real part as $\int_{|x|\le1}\frac{x(\varphi(x)-\varphi(0))}{x^2+\varepsilon^2}dx+\int_{|x|>1}\frac{x\varphi(x)}{x^2+\varepsilon^2}dx$.

steps.slogan: Apply dominated convergence to both pieces of the real part.
steps.detail: For $|x|\le1$ the integrand is bounded by $\sup|\varphi'|$, because $|\varphi(x)-\varphi(0)|\le\sup|\varphi'|\,|x|$ and $x^2/(x^2+\varepsilon^2)\le1$, and it tends to $(\varphi(x)-\varphi(0))/x$. For $|x|>1$ it is bounded by $|\varphi(x)|$, which is integrable, and tends to $\varphi(x)/x$. The limit equals $\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int\varphi/x$, since $\int_{\delta<|x|\le1}\varphi(0)/x\,dx=0$.

steps.slogan: Add the limits of the real and imaginary parts.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 4 give the limits of the two parts of the splitting in step 1. Their sum is $\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int\frac{\varphi(x)}{x}dx\mp i\pi\varphi(0)$.

concepts.c:schwartz-function: Its bounds and decay supply the dominating functions.
concepts.c:cauchy-principal-value: The real part converges to the principal value of $\varphi/x$.
concepts.c:distribution: The limit statement says that $1/(x\pm i0)$ is a distribution.

source.note: The standard distribution-theory computation of the boundary values of $1/(x \pm i\varepsilon)$ with dominated convergence.

statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a [metric space](c:metric-space) with the topology generated by its open [balls](c:ball) $B(x,\varepsilon)$. A set $U\subseteq X$ is [open](c:open-set) if and only if for every $x\in U$ there is $\varepsilon>0$ with $B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq U$.

hypotheses.text: $(X,d)$ is a [metric space](c:metric-space) with the topology generated by its open balls.

conclusion: A set $U$ is open if and only if each point of $U$ is the center of an open ball contained in $U$.

formal.difference: The declaration is stated for a pseudo-metric space, whose topology is defined from the distance through its uniformity. It states the same ball criterion as this statement.

proofs.name: Balls as a neighborhood base
proofs.slogan: Open sets are the sets that are neighborhoods of all their points, and the balls around a point form a neighborhood base there.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The empty set is open and satisfies the ball condition vacuously.

roles.why: The metric gives the balls and the triangle inequality that makes small balls fit inside bigger ones.

steps.slogan: Show that the balls $B(x,\varepsilon)$ form a [neighborhood base](c:neighborhood-base) at each point $x$.
steps.detail: Each ball $B(x,\varepsilon)$ is open and contains $x$. Conversely, an open set $W\ni x$ contains a finite intersection of balls $B(z_j,r_j)$ around $x$; by the triangle inequality $B(x,r_j-d(z_j,x))\subseteq B(z_j,r_j)$, so the smallest of these radii gives a ball around $x$ inside $W$.

steps.slogan: Describe the [neighborhoods](c:neighborhood) of $x$ as the sets that contain a ball around $x$.
steps.detail: A neighborhood $N$ of $x$ contains an open set around $x$, hence a ball $B(x,\varepsilon)$ by step 1. A set that contains such a ball is a neighborhood, because the ball is open.

steps.slogan: Combine with the fact that open sets are neighborhoods of all their points.
steps.detail: A set $U$ is open iff it is a neighborhood of each of its points. By step 2, this holds iff each $x\in U$ has some $\varepsilon>0$ with $B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq U$.

concepts.c:metric-space: The distance defines the balls that generate the topology.
concepts.c:ball: Balls are the basic open sets of the topology.
concepts.c:open-set: The theorem characterizes the open sets by balls.
concepts.c:neighborhood-base: Balls around $x$ form a base of neighborhoods of $x$.
concepts.c:neighborhood: Open sets are exactly the sets that are neighborhoods of all their points.

source.note: mathlib rewrites with isOpen_iff_mem_nhds and Metric.mem_nhds_iff, which comes from nhds_basis_ball (balls form a neighborhood base).

statement: Let $C$ and $C'$ be [compact Riemann surfaces](c:compact-riemann-surface) (smooth complex projective curves) of genus $g\ge2$. If there is an isomorphism of their [Jacobian varieties](c:jacobian-variety) that carries the [theta divisor](c:theta-divisor) of $C$ to a translate of the theta divisor of $C'$, then $C\cong C'$.

hypotheses.text: $C$ and $C'$ are [compact Riemann surfaces](c:compact-riemann-surface) of the same genus $g\ge2$.
An isomorphism $J(C)\to J(C')$ of [Jacobian varieties](c:jacobian-variety) maps the theta divisor of $C$ to a translate of that of $C'$.

proofs.name: Andreotti's Gauss map
proofs.slogan: The Gauss map of the theta divisor has the dual of the canonical curve as branch locus, so the principally polarized Jacobian determines the curve.
proofs.scope: An outline of Andreotti's proof for genus $g\ge2$; steps 3 and 4 rest on the cited paper. Genus 0 and 1 are trivial, and hyperelliptic curves need the separate analysis in the cited paper.

roles.why: The curves supply the symmetric product $C^{(g-1)}$ and the canonical map into $\mathbb{P}^{g-1}$.
The isomorphism transports the theta divisor and its Gauss map, so the branch locus is the same for $C$ and $C'$.

steps.slogan: Identify the [theta divisor](c:theta-divisor) $\Theta$ with the image of $C^{(g-1)}$ in $J(C)$.
steps.detail: By Riemann's theorem, $\Theta$ is a translate of $W_{g-1}$, the image of the Abel-Jacobi map on effective divisors of degree $g-1$. An isomorphism of the principally polarized Jacobians therefore carries $\Theta_C$ to $\Theta_{C'}$.

steps.slogan: Describe the Gauss map of $\Theta$ at a smooth point $D=p_1+\dots+p_{g-1}$.
steps.detail: The tangent hyperplane to $\Theta$ at $D$ is the hyperplane of $\mathbb{P}^{g-1}$ through the canonical images $\varphi_K(p_1),\dots,\varphi_K(p_{g-1})$, that is the unique [canonical divisor](c:canonical-divisor) containing $D$. The Gauss map $\Theta_{\mathrm{sm}}\to(\mathbb{P}^{g-1})^{\vee}$ depends only on $(J,\Theta)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the Gauss map of a non-hyperelliptic curve branches over the dual canonical curve.
steps.detail: A general hyperplane meets the canonical curve in $2g-2$ points, and choosing $g-1$ of them gives $\binom{2g-2}{g-1}$ preimages. The count drops exactly over the hyperplanes tangent to $\varphi_K(C)$, so the branch locus is the dual hypersurface of the canonical curve.

steps.slogan: Recover the canonical curve from the branch locus by biduality.
steps.detail: In characteristic 0 the dual of the dual hypersurface is the original curve. The branch locus is an invariant of $(J,\Theta)$, so it determines $\varphi_K(C)\subset\mathbb{P}^{g-1}$ up to projective equivalence.

steps.slogan: Transfer the isomorphism of canonical models to the curves.
steps.detail: For a non-hyperelliptic curve the canonical map is an isomorphism onto its image, so $C\cong\varphi_K(C)\cong\varphi_{K'}(C')\cong C'$. The degree of the Gauss map differs for hyperelliptic curves, so $C$ is hyperelliptic exactly when $C'$ is; the cited paper treats that case separately.

concepts.c:compact-riemann-surface: The curves are the objects that the theorem recovers.
concepts.c:jacobian-variety: The Jacobian with its polarization is the data that determines $C$.
concepts.c:theta-divisor: The theta divisor carries the Gauss map used in the proof.
concepts.c:canonical-divisor: Tangent hyperplanes of $\Theta$ correspond to canonical divisors of $C$.

source.ref: A. Andreotti, On a theorem of Torelli, American Journal of Mathematics 80 (1958), 801-828
source.note: Andreotti's proof by the Gauss map of the theta divisor; Griffiths and Harris, Principles of Algebraic Geometry, Chapter 2, give an exposition.

statement:
There is an absolute constant $C$ such that every [additive function](c:additive-function) $f\colon\mathbb{N}	o\mathbb{C}$ and every $x\ge2$ satisfy $\sum_{n\le x}|f(n)-A(x)|^2\le C\,x\,B(x)^2$. Here $A(x)=\sum_{p^
u\le x}f(p^
u)p^{-
u}(1- rac1p)$ and $B(x)^2=\sum_{p^
u\le x}|f(p^
u)|^2p^{-
u}$, over powers of [primes](c:prime-number) $p$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [additive](c:additive-function): $f(mn)=f(m)+f(n)$ when $m$ and $n$ are coprime.
The bound $x$ satisfies $x\ge2$.

conclusion: The mean square deviation of $f(n)$ from $A(x)$ over $n\le x$, a [variance](c:variance)-type quantity, is at most $C\,B(x)^2$.

proofs.name: Truncated second moment
proofs.slogan: Truncate $f$ to prime powers up to $x^{1/3}$, compute the second moment of the truncation from sieve counts, and bound the tail by Cauchy-Schwarz.
proofs.scope: All additive $f$ and all $x\ge2$, with an absolute constant whose value is not optimized. Write $q=p^\nu$ for prime powers, $q\,\|\,n$ for $p^\nu$ dividing $n$ exactly, and $\|g\|^2=\sum_{n\le x}|g(n)|^2$.

roles.why: Additivity gives $f(n)=\sum_{q\|n}f(q)$, which expresses $f$ through indicators of exact divisibility.
The condition $x\ge2$ keeps $\log\log x$ bounded below in the Mertens estimate.

steps.slogan: Split $f=f_1+f_2$, where $f_1$ sums over prime powers $q\le y=x^{1/3}$.
steps.detail: By [additivity](c:additive-function), $f(n)=\sum_{q\|n}f(q)$. Put $f_1(n)=\sum_{q\|n,\,q\le y}f(q)$, let $A_1$ be the part of $A(x)$ with $q\le y$, and let $f_2=f-f_1$. Then $\|f-A\|\le\|f_1-A_1\|+\|f_2\|+\|A_1-A\|$.

steps.slogan: Bound the tail $f_2$ and the shift $A-A_1$ by constants times $x\,B(x)^2$.
steps.detail: An integer $n\le x$ has at most two exact prime-power divisors $q>x^{1/3}$, since three of them multiply to more than $x$. So $|f_2(n)|^2\le2\sum_{q\|n,\,q>y}|f(q)|^2$ by Cauchy-Schwarz, and $\|f_2\|^2\le2\sum_q|f(q)|^2\,x/q\le2xB^2$. Also $|A-A_1|^2\le B^2\sum_{y<q\le x}1/q\le cB^2$, because $\sum_{x^{1/3}<p\le x}1/p$ is bounded by Mertens' theorem.

steps.slogan: Count the integers $n\le x$ with $q\,\|\,n$, and with $q\,\|\,n$ and $q'\,\|\,n$ together.
steps.detail: Let $a_q=q^{-1}(1-1/p)$. Then $\#\{n\le x:q\|n\}=x\,a_q+\theta$ with $|\theta|\le1$. For prime powers of different primes, inclusion-exclusion gives $\#\{n\le x:q\|n,\,q'\|n\}=x\,a_qa_{q'}+\theta'$ with $|\theta'|\le2$; for two powers of the same prime the count is 0.

steps.slogan: Expand $\|f_1-A_1\|^2$ and cancel the main terms against $x|A_1|^2$.
steps.detail: Expand $\sum_{n\le x}|f_1(n)|^2=\sum_{q,q'\le y}f(q)\overline{f(q')}N(q,q')$ with the counts of step 3. The main terms are at most $x|A_1|^2$, because same-prime pairs only add a nonnegative sum to $|A_1|^2$. With $\sum_nf_1(n)=xA_1+R$ and $|R|\le S:=\sum_{q\le y}|f(q)|$, the terms $x|A_1|^2-2x|A_1|^2+\lfloor x\rfloor|A_1|^2$ cancel to at most 0, so $\|f_1-A_1\|^2\le xB^2+2S^2+2|A_1|S$.

steps.slogan: Bound $S$ and $A_1$ by Cauchy-Schwarz and add the three norms.
steps.detail: Cauchy-Schwarz with weights $1/q$ gives $S^2\le B^2\sum_{q\le y}q\le B^2x^{2/3}$ and $|A_1|^2\le B^2\sum_{q\le y}1/q\le cB^2(1+\log\log x)$ by Mertens' theorem. So $2S^2+2|A_1|S\le c'xB^2$ and $\|f_1-A_1\|^2\le c''xB^2$. With step 2 and Minkowski's inequality, $\|f-A\|^2\le C\,xB^2$.

concepts.c:additive-function: Additivity writes $f(n)$ as a sum over exact prime-power divisors.
concepts.c:prime-number: The sums and the sieve counts run over prime powers.
concepts.c:variance: The left side is $x$ times the variance of $f$ about $A(x)$.

source.note: Turan's second-moment method; see G. Tenenbaum, Introduction to Analytic and Probabilistic Number Theory, Chapter III.3.

statement: Let $s$ be a set, $(M,d)$ a [metric space](c:metric-space) and $F_n,f\colon s\to M$. Then $F_n\to f$ [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) on $s$ (for the uniformity of $d$) if and only if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $d(f(x),F_n(x))<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$ and $x\in s$; equivalently $\sup_{x\in s}d(f(x),F_n(x))\to0$.

hypotheses.text: $(M,d)$ is a [metric space](c:metric-space), and its uniformity is generated by the sets $\{(a,b):d(a,b)<\varepsilon\}$.
The maps $F_n$ and $f$ send the set $s$ into $M$.

conclusion: Uniform convergence of $F_n$ to $f$ on $s$, the $\varepsilon$-$N$ criterion and $\sup_{x\in s}d(f(x),F_n(x))\to0$ are equivalent.

formal.difference: The declaration equates the entourage definition with the epsilon criterion for a pseudo-emetric space and an arbitrary filter on the index set. It does not state the supremum form, which step 3 adds.

proofs.name: Entourages and balls
proofs.slogan: Entourages of a metric uniformity contain sets $\{d<\varepsilon\}$, so uniform convergence is the $\varepsilon$-$N$ criterion, which says that the supremum distance tends to 0.
proofs.scope: Sequences $F_n$ with $n\in\mathbb{N}$. The supremum may be $+\infty$ for small $n$; the claim only concerns large $n$.

roles.why: The metric uniformity has the sets $\{d<\varepsilon\}$ as a base, which links entourages and $\varepsilon$.
Common domain $s$ makes the supremum over $x\in s$ meaningful.

steps.slogan: Apply the definition to the entourage $\{(a,b):d(a,b)<\varepsilon\}$.
steps.detail: Each set $E_\varepsilon=\{(a,b):d(a,b)<\varepsilon\}$ with $\varepsilon>0$ is an entourage of the metric uniformity. [Uniform convergence](c:uniform-convergence) therefore gives $N$ with $(f(x),F_n(x))\in E_\varepsilon$, that is $d(f(x),F_n(x))<\varepsilon$, for all $n\ge N$ and $x\in s$.

steps.slogan: Show that every entourage of the metric uniformity contains some $E_\varepsilon$.
steps.detail: The sets $E_\varepsilon$ generate the metric uniformity, so every entourage $U$ contains some $E_\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. The $\varepsilon$-$N$ criterion for this $\varepsilon$ gives $N$ with $(f(x),F_n(x))\in E_\varepsilon\subseteq U$ for all $n\ge N$ and $x\in s$, so the convergence is uniform.

steps.slogan: Show that the $\varepsilon$-$N$ criterion is equivalent to $\sup_xd(f(x),F_n(x))\to0$.
steps.detail: If $d(f(x),F_n(x))<\varepsilon$ for all $x\in s$ and $n\ge N$, then the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) is at most $\varepsilon$ for $n\ge N$. Conversely, if the supremum is below $\varepsilon$ for $n\ge N$, then $d(f(x),F_n(x))<\varepsilon$ for every $x\in s$.

steps.slogan: Chain the three conditions into one cycle of equivalences.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 show that uniform convergence and the $\varepsilon$-$N$ criterion imply each other. Step 3 links the criterion with the supremum form, so all three conditions are equivalent.

concepts.c:metric-space: The distance $d$ defines the entourages and the supremum distance.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: It is the property that the proof characterizes.
concepts.c:least-upper-bound: The supremum distance is the sup-norm quantity that tends to 0.
